comments.author: jdub
comments.text: Instead of post-processing the binary to add the application (non-SELF) schema, you could run database migrations before servicing requests. Thus, every time you start the process, the app creates and/or upgrades its own schema. The SELF upgrade (heh, self upgrade) and rollback processes could benefit from some... fancier... footwork. Your example has a new binary copying old data into it, but then you have to move the new binary to the deployed location. Which means an outage through stop service, data migration, replace file, start service. What if the upgrade process was more like... write the new SELF data into the old binary, send SIGHUP, and then the service fork+execs itself, while doing haproxy-like zero downtime FD handover? Replacing the SELF data in the existing file is safe right now, because you can't mmap segments into memory. But if you do end up figuring out some clever BLOB alignment mmap stuff, you could do the SELF upgrade like a data migration! INSERT segments/symbols, fork+exec, and the data migration cleans out the old code. :-D Updating the SELF schema to allow multiple sets of segments and symbols would allow for this upgrade trick, but could do other fancy things... thin multi-arch binaries where only the code segments differ. BLOB alignment should also mean more efficient static asset serving and a bunch of other niceties... definitely worthy of investigation. However -- very strong however -- as fun as this is, I would never, ever, ever allow an internet-facing service binary to be self-writable. :-)

comments.text: > Black hole singularity is a surface not a point Might they be trying to say this? 1. In models of black holes, there is a gravitational singularity at a point in the centre: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_singularity which is a topic with nuances.

comments.author: tialaramex
comments.text: This idiocy is a big part of why it was so important to get Python people working on TLS implementations to understand that the defined mechanism for SANs (no the "alternative" in Subject Alternative Name doesn't mean in the sense of more than one, X.509 is originally for the X.500 system and the Internet repurposed X.509 so these are alternative names from the Internet) says that these are DNS names, they specifically are not to be understood as some sort of human readable text, and thus "decoding" them to Unicode is definitely nonsense even though Python really wanted to do that and I think used to do it or at least proposed to. The rule for how SAN DnsNames match againt like names, from the DNS is very, very simple so that you don't screw it up. You handle a single wildcard (ASCII * code 42 matches any single DNS label) and beyond that it's literally byte comparison. You don't care what these bytes mean, either the bytes are all identical or that's not a match and we're done.

comments.author: ummonk
comments.text: > The fix was to create new exceptions so that str.lower() would behave as if it was using Unicode 3.2.0 for only particular function. So, we go through each Unicode codepoint and record when the behavior of str.lower() is different when comparing the Unicode version shipped with Python and Unicode 3.2.0 This sounds like a really hacky solution compared to implementing a separate frozen Unicode 3.2.0 lower.

stories.title_en: C2PA Cameras Do Not Survive Contact with Reality

comments.author: mistercow
comments.text: Aside from the fact that this was obviously never viable and the entire problem is clearly unsolvable if you sit down and really probe it for fifteen minutes, what I find most frustrating about this is that the false promise of preserving photos as reliable evidence is actively harmful. You will not build a perfect system, or even something near perfect. The best you're going to do is make it so that it's hard to casually present AI photos as real, leaving only the cases where it really matters. In the "best" case, you've just made the public more trusting of photos in general, so that when there's actual money or power on the line that makes jumping through the hoops to fake authenticity worth it, the public is more susceptible. The best outcome at this point is for everyone to get on the same page that photos have roughly the same probative value now as drawings. Poorly thought out snake oil efforts to prove authenticity are only going to delay that.

comments.author: trentor

Our agency signed a insurance not only because of clients who don't want to use AI in their artwork but also because of the EU AI act. They c2pa to get their money back from a cheating supplier if they are not compliant with the AI act.

stories.summary_ja: C2PA は実際には機能せず、偽の信頼性を与えることで悪影響を及ぼす。完璧な偽造防止は不可能で、せいぜい気軽な AI 画像の偽装を難しくするだけ。それにより一般の写真への信頼が高まり、金銭や権力が関わる場面ではよりだまされやすくなる。本当の解決策は写真を絵と同じ証拠価値とみなすこと。実際には広告や EU AI 法のコンプライアンスのために使われ、RAW ワークフローでの provenance 確認の方が現実的だ。C2PA の本来の目的とメディアの期待にズレがある。

comments.author: wraptile
comments.text: I'm a scuba diver here in Thailand and you can still see blast fishing damage from decades ago that never fully recovered. It's truly as terrible as the article makes it out to be. What is interesting is that both Indonesia and Thailand have strong and similar anti blast fishing laws since early 00s that charge 5+ years of prison time. However, Thailand has been much more successful with taming blast fishing which is practically gone now and the story here is very insightful. Some of it is due to Thailand's geography and high demand for marine tourism but the biggest push here was EU and US regulation that gave Thailand opportunity to shape up. In 2015 (same year when Thai anti blast laws were codified more strictly) US TIP (trafficking in persons) report down-graded Thailand to tier 3 mostly due to fishing slave workers while at the same time EU's IUU (illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing) issued a yellow card. All of which lead to the biggest fishery reform in Thai history which mostly eliminated blast fishing. Since then Thailand is back to tier 2 of TIP and got lost the yellow card from EU's IUU. Indonesia never got tier 3 of TIP despite many arguing it should have and never got a card from IUU. Stories like this turn me into a globalization believer - I know it's not perfect but the system is kinda working?

stories.title_en: Run OpenBSD on DigitalOcean for $4/month
stories.title_ja: 月額4ドルでDigitalOcean上でOpenBSDを実行

comments.author: bananamogul
comments.text: That pricing is awful. $4/month for 512MB VPS...eeek. You'll find much better pricing at RackNerd, DediRock, InterServer, BuyVM, etc. Small indy hosting companies are the way to go. 2GB for $5/month or so is the typical price point. Any host that offers KVM and allows you to upload your own ISO can run OpenBSD (or FreeBSD, NetBSD, whatever you want). Check out LowEndTalk or LowEndBox for deals. There are other sites but that's where I shop. Sure, if you need an API, or if you want to host in one of the less common locations, or if you absolutely must have five nines, then DO or Vultr or Linode or Amazon LightSail can be a good fit. But if you just need a VPS with a control panel in a typical hosting location (Amsterdam, LA, New York, Chicago, Singapore, etc.) then I don't see the point of paying more at one of the big hosts.

comments.author: ninjin
comments.text: Always happy to see more people having fun with OpenBSD. Running my own set of OpenBSD boxes (although the public-facing ones are on Hetzner), so I read through the instructions and it aligns with my own experience (although I usually emphasise that most correct choices in the installer are just the default). However, this part: "Since this is going to be a bare-bones web server we can remove most of the sets.". This is not great advice. Reducing the number of sets even on a headless server can lead to issues with ports depending on libraries Xenocara provides that would then be missing (fonts, etc.). Likewise, when you upgrade the default is to install all sets unless you manually intervene, which could lead to a surprise bump in disk usage that you may not have accounted for. In general, reducing the number of sets should be considered "I am deviating from the defaults and I know what I am doing" territory and Theo keeps threatening to remove the option to select the sets in the installer when people complain and I am inclined to agree with him. So, if you have 10GB of disk in that Droplet, just do the OpenBSD thing and go with the defaults and you will be all the happier for it down the line. Messing with the installation size really is for those rare cases (fitting many VMs on a single host, ancient machines, etc.) where you have no other choice.

comments.author: kslambert
comments.text: Author here. Thanks for the comments everyone! There are many comments on the price point. I would like to comment on one thing. "$20k is too much" I agree $20k is an investment. Could I have done it for cheaper? Absolutely. Would a DIY shell been cheaper? Would doing more of the work myself have been cheaper? Could I have saved by putting in the smaller stock windows and not having a skylight? Of course! But I am a dad with a young kid, he was 1 when I built the office. I didn't want to spend my limited free time on this project. There was a trade-off between paying for labor and the time it would take to do it myself. At this point in my life I always look at these decisions through a lens of: is the cost savings worth my time. In this case I valued my time more than the cost savings. I was lucky enough to be in a situation where I would rather spend money for someone else to build this then spending my nights and weekends on this project. I am almost 4 years in I would have paid over $20k for a co-working space. We were able to stay in our smaller house with a ridiculously low mortgage rate. We made the right choice for us. Cheap is relative. Sometimes your time is worth more. There are litteraly entire companies built on this premise, cough DoorDash

comments.author: ryandrake
comments.text: For work-from-home, I can't emphasize enough how much of a game changer it is to have a physically separate building for your work, especially if you have a family with kids and noise and pets and things. Working from a spare bedroom, even one without a bed / outfitted as an office, is just not my thing. Even if your family "knows the rules" and let you work in peace. It subjectively still "feels like you're home". With a separate building, I can do a short walking commute and take those 10 seconds to "get into work mindset." And, once I'm out there, it can be a hermetically sealed, zero-distraction zone. If you are lucky and fortunate enough to live in an actual house with land, and work (or are thinking about working) remotely, seriously consider investing in an actual separate building for your office.

comments.author: amiga386
comments.text: 12935 -> TIZZY (5625) -> OXBOW (2674) -> GRUFF (858) -> MAMMA (195) and I'll let you guess the rest but my next choice left 43 words, and I survived with only 4 words possible. The rules not letting use a letter you know isn't in the target word drastically cuts your choices, your best bet is to use as few unique letters per word as you can, and as uncommon letters as you can, but as all normal words need vowels you'll be forced into only picking a vowel from the target word soon enough. Try to find letters that are in the word as late as possible so you're not locked into having to use them. Once you are forced to use letters from the target word, avoid placing them in the right place. Sadly there's a rule not letting you use a known letter more than once in a word (once A is known, you can't write ALPHA), and a rule for not letting you put a known letter in a place you know it doesn't go (so after MAMMA, you can't have HALVE because you know there's not an A in second place, nor ALPHA because you know there's not an A in fifth place).

comments.text: That was a very interesting read. I've always wondered about the details around the contract between the big ski resorts and the NFS, fun to read the actual permit. Ikon and Vail seem to be a duopoly and the geographical limitations inherent of a ski resort make the free-market argument hard to believe - you can't just open up a new resort next to breck or vail and charge lower rates. I was a long time epic/ikon pass holder - I didn't buy one last year, and I bought a smaller resort's season pass directly this year. Let it snow!

comments.author: ramesh31
comments.text: On the other hand allowing the high window prices and holiday pricing are what drive the ability for these companies to make the massive capital investments that they have, while season pass prices have plummeted for anyone local that actually skis a lot. It's not just rent seeking; a lift ticket today is fundamentally a far superior product to what was being sold in the 70s, and nobody but gapers are paying full retail. Let them subsidize it for us I say.

stories.summary_ja: 記事はスキー場とNFSの契約や、Ikon・Vailのデュオポリーによる市場制約、高額ウィンドウ価格とホリデー価格が大規模投資を可能にし、ローカルのシーズンパス価格は下降していることを議論している。

comments.text: With both Firefox and Chromium using jxl-rs (Rust-based), I wonder what Apple will do about the libjxl (C++) they already shipped. I also wonder if anyone's done benchmark comparisons between both libs. -- Also, I was under the impression that after backtracking, Chromium was relying on Mozilla to come up with a Rust port, but it seems it was the reverse. Good on Google Research. https://hacks.mozilla.org/2026/08/intent-to-ship-jpeg-xl/ > So, we laid down a challenge to the JPEG XL team at Google Research: Build a safe, performant, compact, and compatible JPEG XL decoder in Rust, and we’ll ship it. That challenge was met; Google Research built jxl-rs, and it’s the core of our JPEG XL support in Firefox.

stories.title_en: Tracking Costco gas prices
stories.title_ja: コストコのガソリン価格を追跡

comments.author: jopolous
comments.text: I worked at Costco while in college many years ago and I got to see how the gas price was set for my specific warehouse. Someone would drive out to a few neighboring gas stations, record prices, and set ours ~10 cents lower. That’s it. That’s how the price was set. Aside, working there was very good for a college job and I was treated very respectfully for the summers I was there.

comments.author: culi
comments.text: GasBuddy is great for this. You can see average gas prices across all gas stations for a certain region (or nation-wide). https://www.gasbuddy.com/charts The data goes back even over 25 years if you play around with the query params (it started in June of 2000). E.g. https://charts.gasbuddy.com/ch.gaschart?Country=USA&Crude=f&...

comments.author: xp84
comments.text: > "a Global Fuel Crisis" Does anyone else find this hyperbolic? Gas prices here in the US are up about 26% from their recent-past price -- it stayed in a very narrow range of about $3.20 for a year or two, and now is at $4.05. A "FUEL CRISIS" is what you are seeing in Moscow right now. People lined up for miles and sometimes when you get to the front the delivery does not happen because the refinery got blown up. Or at least the 1970s oil crisis. A 26% bump in prices is a major annoyance, not a "crisis." I would guess that the person who wrote this headline has some kind of a political agenda. Did he describe it as a "fuel crisis" when gas prices rose from their previous ~2.80 baseline to the peak of $4.93 in June 2022, a 76% increase? Or was it not a crisis then for some reason?

comments.author: walrus01
comments.text: I don't see any need to 'track' costco gas prices in my area, because at least in western washington state, my local costco is always the least expensive option for regular unleaded. My choice of whether I go there to fill up is simply if it happens to be on the way to/from somewhere else I'm going or is not an unreasonable detour. Or I need to do some other costco shopping. Or it's late at night and the costco is closed, so I have to go to a 24x7 place like an ARCO. The gas price savings easily pays for the annnual standard costco membership.

comments.author: 0cf8612b2e1e
comments.text: Costco gas is famously a loss leader, typically running 15 to 20 cents below surrounding stations. Is this true? I always assumed that Costco just had better deals/longer horizon commitments so it could undercut local stations. Maybe they even own a refinery just to maintain the best margin.

stories.summary_ja: コストコのガソリン価格は近隣駅を調べて10セントほど低く設定され、多くの利用者が最安値だと感じている。GasBuddyで地域別価格を追えるが、「燃料危機」という表現は過大だと指摘がある。価格追跡の必要性については意見が分かれる。
